I -wish to briDg before the minister a matter about which I have had some correspondence with him from a different angle. It is a matter to which I think Canada owes some consideration. I refer to the case of those men who took pensions from the Pacific cable board, or rather from their successors, entitled International Communications Company, Limited. The situation is this. As the house may remember, the Pacific cable board was jointly owned by Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand and Canada in certain proportions, and the board operated a cable to Australia. For reasons which I need not go into they decided to sell out, which they did some years ago to the International Communications Company, Limited. I would refer to the debate on the subject in this house when the matter came up on May 14, 1929. I then stated that the Canadian terminal of the cable was in the constituency I represented at a place called Bamfield,
and I wanted to know if the employees of the board who entered its service somewhat as one would enter the government service here, with an understanding as to continuity of service, pension and so forth, would in the transfer have their rights as to continuity of service, pension and so forth safeguarded. The Postmaster General said that that provision was to be found in the agreement signed by the contracting parties. There was some debate about it, in which the member for Acadia took part, and further on the Postmaster General said:
The agreement provides that the company shall take over the existing staff of the board subject to and in accordance with the provisions set out in the second schedule thereof.
The Postmaster General went on to say that the rights of these employees were fully protected by the agreement to which I have referred. Following that up, the Postmaster General sent me a letter dated May 15, enclosing the second schedule of the agreement, and I want to comment on one or two of its clauses. Subsection 1 of section 2 thereof says that the company would employ the old employees of the Pacific cable board on at least as favourable terms as those they had been enjoying. Then it came to the question of those who, owing to the changed conditions, did not wish to continue with the new company but decided to take their rights of pension and so forth under the old board; there was a period of five years allowed during which they could exercise that right, and this is what was to happen if they did so exercise it. I quote:
The company

I differentiate between the board and the company, the board being the old organization and the company the new one. It provides that the company will pay to any man quitting under those conditions,-
-compensation of such amount by way of pension, gratuity or otherwise, as he would have received from any pension or provident fund of the board or from the board itself in accordance with its usual practice if he had retired on grounds of ill health from the service of the board.
Section 4 provided that any dispute between any employee of the company should be referred to the decision of a single arbitrator to be appointed by the Lord Chief Justice of England. That was the old provision.
To put the matter shortly, the trouble arose because faith was not kept with these employees in the matter of their pensions. I quote now from one of these employees' letters:
Supply-Post Office

The following rule was made by the board (the old board) on March 22, 1922, prior to the payment of the first pension in Canada on March 31, 1922.
This is the rule:
It has been decided that as the pension fund is not a trust fund payments made in Canada on account of pensions or death gratuities will be at the standard rate of $4.87 to the pound and not at current rate.
This letter continues:
This rule was displayed for our information at the time we notified the company that we did not wish to transfer to it, and was not rescinded at the time we retired; this definite assurance influenced our decision to retire.
As indeed it well might. It goes on:
The company now states that this ruling is obsolete as the pension fund was constituted a trust fund on December 17, 1923, and that the regulations date from that time.
The company changed it?
The remarks of the hon. member are very interesting, but I must say the matter does not come under my department; it concerns a private British company.

The minister has not appreciated my point; I suggest it does come under his jurisdiction. These men were in his employ-or in our employ, if you like. We
traded them off without their knowledge or consent to a British corporation. We stipulated that in so doing that corporation must take care of those men under the terms at the time of their enlistment. They acquired a very valuable franchise and property from us.
That was under the Postmaster General.

It was the Postmaster General who made the contract. Hansard reveals where I asked the question, "Are those men going to be protected?" And the Postmaster General replied, "Yes, I have protected them. They come under the second schedule to this agreement." Although the Prime Minister is not in his seat he could support me in my statement that I had urged that the agreement be made part of the act. I foresaw the day might come when the bargain would be under consideration. The present Prime Minister supported me in my view, and arrangement was made by the then Minister of Justice to insert it. It is certainly our business to see that Canadian subjects are treated properly, especially when we have traded them off in that way. We should follow them up and see that the deal we made on their behalf is fulfilled.

Perhaps I can make an
explanation which would help to clear matters. I think it was in 1929 that Canada relinquished her claims or rights to the cable system in which she was then interested. In that was included the cable to Cuba.
We were owners of part of it.

We were paid so much, in the end. In relinquishing her claim, however, Canada entered into an agreement with this corporation by which they were to protect the men then employed so far as pensions were concerned. I take it the Postmaster General has jurisdiction to see that that agreement is being carried out.
Hear, hear.

That is as far ias he can go. I would ask the Postmaster General to have the matter looked into carefully toy the Justice department to see wherein this corporation has failed in carrying out the agreement which was scheduled to the act at the time.
The question is under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, 'before entering into discussion of post office estimates in their details, perhaps the committee will allow me to give a summary of the main operations of the department. I do not intend at this moment to take up the time of the committee with an explanation of details, but in the course of discussion I shall be glad to give any information which may be called for by the committee.
The Post Office estimates show a decrease of 84,688,875 from those of the preceding year. This has been effected by reducing every one of the four main items, and indicates a real endeavour to balance revenue and expenditure during the fiscal year 1932-33. The important point in connection with these estimates is that the total is lower than for any year since 1925-28 as the result of drastic cuts. In fact the total reduction in post office estimates during the past two years is more than six millions of dollars.
Turning for a moment to the question of revenue and expenditure, I might say for the information of the committee that an encouraging factor in connection with the financial position of the Post Office Department is a marked reduction in expenditure. According to the latest figures available, the expenditure for the fiscal year which closed on the 31st March, 1932, will not exceed $34,315,000, a decrease of over $1,975,000 as compared with the fiscal year 1930-31. Another factor is that the revenue for the fiscal year which closed on the 31st March last is estimated to be over $31,900,000, an increase of nearly $1,500,000 over the fiscal year 1930-31. In the latter year the deficit in postal operations was $5,876,496, but for the fiscal year which has just closed it is estimated that the deficit will not exceed $2,368,000, a reduction of over $3,500,000 in one year.

mit'tee, and the deficit which has existed for several years past will have been wiped out in a period of two years.
In view of the policy that the post office operates for service and not profit, I do not consider it necessary that the postal service should show any marked surplus, 'but a deficit is undesirable, and I wish to assure the committee that every endeavour is being made in the administration of the department to render the best possible service at the lowest possible cost.
The reduction in revenue, caused by business depression, forced me to reduce the cost of the air mail service to $225,000 from $1,300,000, which was the figure for 1931-32, a reduction of $1,075,000. This reduction was not effected for pleasure but from necessity. It is usually much more agreeable to grant than to refuse. In these times of depression the task of reducing expenses, salaries and the number of employees, is extremely painful and presents a problem which, not being entirely solved, demands prudence and the greatest foresight. A great portion of these reductions are but temporary. It will be necessaty, however, to limit expenses in future, taking into account not only the government's finances, but the real needs of the country, as well as the various other means of transportation which have absorbed huge amounts of public funds due to previous lack of forethought.

Before going into any
questions with the minister, may I be permitted to refer briefly to the remarks he has just made. Let me say at the outset, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is quite right when he states that the Post Office Department should not be run with a view to showing a marked surplus. Let me add that in 1927 when the reduction in the cost of postage from three cents to two cents showed that for some time there would be a considerable deficit each year, I as Postmaster General brought the matter before the house. It was fully discussed, and the opinion was then expressed that, no matter what that deficit might be, while it would be well to balance our accounts as soon as possible, yet the mail service should not be allowed to depreciate in any way.
With that object in view I proceeded to lay out a program for the development of greater service in Canada, and without boasting at all I think I can say I was successful to a considerable extent in giving Canada, from 1927 to 1929 and 1930, one of the best mail services of any country in the world. I

feel proud of that. I do not take the credit to myself personally as minister; I freely give it to the energetic, efficient and industrious staff who assisted me. They considered public service the very first thing that should be attended to. The extension of mail routes by train to sections of the three prairie provinces and British Columbia entailed a heavy expenditure, but both sides of the house were unanimous in authorizing the then Postmaster General to proceed with the work, after the program was laid out and it was shown that there would be deficits.
In addition we inaugurated an air mail service, and on that point permit me to say that I am indeed disappointed that the government has seen fit almost completely to destroy the foundation then laid for air mail service in Canada. It is true that the service was costly, but when I spoke on this subject last year I had facts and figures which I laid before the committee and by which I showed that if the services were continued the deficit would become less each year. At that time it appeared that the services would be continued, because the estimate for 1931-32 was no less than $1,500,000 or a little more than the estimate for 1930-31. It was believed all over the country that these services would be carried on, but we have seen what has happened. I am not blaming the Postmaster General for this, nor am I blaming any official of his department; the government as a whole must take the responsibility and the blame for what has been done.
What has been the result? At that time I pointed out that if the services were carried on over the routes then established, the worst that could happen would be a deficit for all the routes of about $390,000. It must not be forgotten that week by week, month by month and year by year the volume of business carried by the air mail was increasing. In 1930 it increased by more than 25 per cent, and it had not fallen off at the end of the fiscal year, 1931, when the then government brought in an estimate of $1,500,000 as the amount necessary to carry on the sendee. If it had been carried on this year as fully as was anticipated when that estimate was brought down, with the increase to three cents on what was known as the two cent air mail services there would have been an increase in revenue of about $190,000. The increase from five cents to six cents on what was known as the five cent routes also would have brought in a large increase. Let the department take the figures, and what will they find? They will find that every two cent route, such as the Magdalen islands
route, the north shore route to Anticosti and the Mackenzie river route to the Arctic circle, as well as the routes to isolated mining districts, showed a surplus for the year. There was a deficit of $650,000 on the five cent routes, but as I said a moment ago the traffic was increasing, and there was every reason to hope that this year the deficit would not have been more than from $350,000 to $390,000.
Now let me put this point: The United States, with a deficit of over two billion dollars, and a deficit of $60,000,000 on postal service, is not cutting down the air mail service. Great Britain, with millions of a deficit, is not cutting down either. Why is that? It is because Great Britain sees in the air mail service, just as we in the former government saw in the Canadian air mail service, a connecting link of empire, a connecting link with Europe, and ultimately a transatlantic service of which Canada would be the pivotal point on this continent. We saw that; we had the information in our possession, but that program has been dropped, though these other two countries are spending large sums of money on their air mail service in spite of their deficit. An immense amount of work was done and large sums of money were invested in order to carry out this program in Canada. There was a great forward movement in civil aviation of which postal aviation was the groundwork and foundation, because without it commercial aviation cannot be carried on in Canada. All that has gone by the board. Companies invested millions of dollars in equipping themselves to carry air mail, with the encouragement of the government, but to-day they see the capital they invested going to waste. The machines that they bought for that service cannot last until the government decides, two or three years hence, that an improvement in conditions will allow them once more to go on with the service. If any service in the country is essential to the progress of Canada it is the mail service of the Post Office Department; there is no question about that. Take, for instance, its effect with regard to other countries. When we lowered the rate to the Argentine Republic in 1929-we not only lowered the rate on first class matter but we raised the poundage of parcel post, extended it and reduced the rate-an additional revenue of nearly $200,000 was brought to the department. And when Canada was placed on the penny postage rate with England the department secured additional revenue. Now the rate has been raised to three cents and that advantage has been lost. If any account could be obtained with regard to mail com-

munication between Canada and foreign countries, you would find that the service has been going down since the increase in postage. I predicted, when the increase in postage was put on, that the value of postage going through the mails would be affected, not so much by the depression as by the fact that we were imposing an additional tax upon those who could write; for people who can post eight letters for sixteen cents are not going to write four letters on which they will have to pay twelve cents. When the rate was raised on newspapers from one to one and a half cents per pound, the department lost revenue, and this revenue was lost by the shortsightedness not of the officials of the department nor of the minister but of those who undertook governmental retrenchment in a department of which they had no real knowledge or experience. The revenue from newspaper postage has declined notwithstanding the increase of one half cent per pound. The Montreal Star circulates three thousand papers in this city alone, but these papers are not being sent through the post as formerly, because the increase would cost the Star $80,000. To-day they are sending packages to distribution stations in Ottawa and elsewhere, not by the mail, as they did under the one cent rate, but by express; and within a radius of fifty miles of the great cities of Canada all the large newspapers are making more use of trucks and express, sending their papers to district news agents. They are using these conveyances more than they did under the one cent rate. We have lost revenue there by want of foresight, of judgment and of a proper discussion and understanding of the situation. I predict that the revenue lost by the mail service on newspapers alone will amount to over $225,000 a year.
It was in 1928, I think, that, as Postmaster General, I introduced a bill in this house reducing the rate on newspapers from a cent and a half to one cent. What was the result? In the next year there was an additional revenue of $250,000 from newspapers alone, and we are losing that now since we have raised the rate to a cent and a half. So that it is not always wise to increase rates; it does not always bring the expected volume of business. Very often it has the opposite effect, lowering the volume of business done by the department.
